newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: More courtroom drama seen for Australian pay-TV.
newsitem.headline: More courtroom drama seen for Australian pay-TV.

text.p: Australia's money-losing pay-television industry appears to be heading for another court battle following the announcement of a proposed merger between Australis Media Ltd and rival Foxtel, partly owned by News Corp.
Optus Vision, the other player in the industry, has already denounced the proposed tie-up, unveiled late on Friday.

Optus, owned by Optus Communications Pty Ltd, would not comment on Monday on whether it had started legal proceedings but analysts said legal action was likely and a formal announcement was expected later this week.

The legal moves could potentially block the merger, which would create Australia's largest pay-TV group. Foxtel is equally owned by Rupert Murdoch's The News Corp Ltd and the Australian government's telecommunications carrier, Telstra Corp Ltd.
Legal action would also complicate the proposed partial float of Telstra, scheduled for November, but analysts said a delay of the float seemed unlikely at this stage.
The public share offer of a third of Telstra is expected to raise at least A$8 billion (US$5.8 billion) for government coffers, but analysts tip the total raised would be far higher.
Legal action by Optus was likely to be aimed at winning an agreement from Foxtel over programming, analysts said.
"Optus clearly does not want to be cut out totally and it probably has a plan up it sleeve already," said one media industry analyst.

Optus, which is 49 percent owned by Britain's Cable and Wireless Plc, has already said it will complain to competition regulator, the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission (ACCC), about the merger on the basis that it would reduce industry competition.

Analysts said that if the merger went ahead, future talks between Optus and merged group over further industry rationalisation would be on Foxtel's terms as it will have the bulk of programming rights and subscribers.
Under terms of the proposed merger, Foxtel will take a 66.5 percent stake in Australis. The merger would also give the enlarged group the bulk of Australia's pay-TV subscribers.
Foxtel currently has about 200,000 subscribers, Australis about 110,000 and Optus about 180,000.
This is the second attempt by Australis and Foxtel to merge.
The first deal was killed off by the ACCC in January 1996 on anti-competitive grounds.
ACCC chairman Alan Fels said on Sunday that conditions had changed since then but he stopped short of saying the current proposal would be approved.
Fels said the industry was now well established whereas it was in a startup stage with the first deal was vetoed.
The deal is unlikely to be blocked. "I can't really see why they would rule against it," said a telecommunications analyst.
Rationalisation in the industry has long been touted.
The three major players have lost a total of about A$2 billion since 1993 and profits are unlikely for a long time yet.
"Any rationalisation has got to be good in terms of heading towards profitability," said the Sydney-based telecoms analyst.
Australia's pay-TV sector has seen a spate of court room battles involving each industry player, many fought over programming and ownership issues.
